opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that engineers need to get much better at *specifying* what they want. With a human colleague, you can be a bit vague, and they'll come back with questions, or they'll fill in the gaps using context they've built up over months of working with you. With these models, the quality of what you get back is heavily tied to how clearly you've described the problem: what the inputs and outputs are, what the edge cases are, what performance characteristics matter, how it should fit into the existing system. So, in a way, writing a good spec, or a good design doc, becomes even more valuable than it was before.

The second thing is to think of the model less as an autocomplete and more as a collaborator you can delegate to, but one you still need to check. You want to set things up so verification is cheap. Good tests are a big part of that. If you have a solid test suite, you can let the model take bigger swings, because you'll quickly know whether what it produced actually works. If you don't, you end up reading every line very carefully, and a lot of the productivity gain disappears.

And I'd say decompose the problem well. Engineers who are good at breaking a large system into well-defined pieces with clean interfaces tend to get much more out of these tools, because each piece is something the model can handle well on its own. That's always been a good software engineering skill, but it's becoming even more important.

Finally, I'd encourage people to experiment, and to keep re-evaluating. The capabilities are changing quickly. Something that didn't work six months ago might work quite well now. So if you tried it once, decided it wasn't useful for your kind of work, and never looked again, you're probably leaving a lot on the table. The people who will benefit most are the ones who keep adjusting how they work as the models get better.

r001.rationale: It says the quality of the model’s output depends heavily on how clearly the engineer describes the task.

r002.rationale: It discusses delegation and decomposing tasks, but does not say the appropriate interaction frequency depends on the task.

r003.rationale: It connects clear specifications with delegating work to the model and says well-defined pieces are tasks the model can handle on its own.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful mental shift is to stop treating these models as a fancier autocomplete and start treating them more like a very fast, very well-read collaborator who has zero context about your particular problem until you give it to them. A lot of the disappointing interactions I see come from people typing a one-line request and then being surprised the result doesn't match the thing in their head. If you handed that same one-liner to a new engineer on day one, you'd get the same mismatch.

So the first thing is: spend the tokens on context. Tell the model what the system is, what the constraints are, what you've already tried, what "done" looks like. Point it at the relevant parts of the codebase. The models are really good at absorbing a lot of information quickly, and the quality of what comes back scales pretty directly with the quality of what you put in.

The second thing is to think in terms of decomposition. The same instinct that makes you a good engineer when you break a hard problem into pieces you can reason about applies here. Ask for a plan before asking for the code. Have it write the tests first, or at least agree on what the tests should be. Then let it fill in the pieces. When you do that, you get something you can actually review, instead of a two-thousand-line diff you have to take on faith.

And that gets to the third thing, which is that you shouldn't abdicate judgment. The model can generate a lot of plausible code very fast, and plausible is not the same as correct. I think the role of the engineer shifts toward being the person who owns the design, owns the verification, and owns the taste. Is this the right abstraction? Is this going to be maintainable? Does this actually handle the edge cases that matter for our users? Those are still your questions to answer. The model can help you answer them, but it won't know which ones matter unless you tell it.

I'd also say be a little experimental. These tools are changing on the order of months, not years, and the right workflow six months ago is probably not the right workflow today. People who are getting the most out of them are the ones who keep poking at the boundaries of what they can hand off, noticing where it works and where it breaks, and adjusting. There's a real skill in learning the shape of what a model is good at, and that skill is learned by doing, not by reading about it.

The last thing I'd say is to be aware of what you might be losing. When I was learning to program, a lot of the understanding came from the struggle, from stepping through things and building a mental model of why they behaved a certain way. If the model does all of that for you, you can end up with working code and no model in your own head. For a senior person who already has that, it's a pure win. For someone earlier in their career, I'd encourage deliberately keeping some of the struggle, at least on the things you want to deeply understand. Use the model to go faster on the stuff you already know, and use it as a tutor rather than a replacement on the stuff you don't.

r001.rationale: It says the model starts with no context and that the quality of its response scales with the context and information the engineer provides.

r002.rationale: It discusses adapting workflows and deciding what to hand off, but does not state that interaction frequency should depend on the task.

r003.rationale: It recommends providing context and constraints and letting the model fill in pieces, but does not clearly say that sufficiently clear task specification is what enables independent delegation.

astra-6.text:
I think engineers should get comfortable working at a higher level of abstraction. Instead of specifying every line of code, you describe what you want to accomplish, the constraints that matter, and how you’ll know whether the result is correct. That ability to communicate intent clearly becomes really valuable.

And it should be an iterative interaction. Ask the model to propose an approach, look at the tradeoffs, and then have it implement a piece you can test. If something is wrong, give it concrete feedback. You don’t want to simply accept a large amount of code because it looks plausible.

The engineering judgment is still yours: Are we solving the right problem? Is this interface sensible? What happens when something fails? The models can help with those questions, too, but being able to evaluate their answers is an important part of using them well.

r001.rationale: It says engineers should communicate goals, constraints, and correctness criteria, then describes how to use that input to guide the model’s approach, implementation, and revisions.

r002.rationale: It recommends iterative interaction but does not say the appropriate frequency depends on the task.

r003.rationale: It recommends clear task descriptions, but does not present sufficient clarity as a basis for delegating execution independently; it instead describes a guided, iterative process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to get comfortable working at different levels of abstraction. Sometimes you want to ask a model to write a small function. Other times you want to describe a larger goal and have it propose a design before you start implementing things.

In either case, being clear about what you want matters a lot. What are the constraints? What does success look like? What existing code should it fit into? And then you want a feedback loop: look at what it produces, run tests, and refine the request. Treat the output as something to examine, rather than assuming that because it looks plausible, it’s correct.

That shifts some of the engineer’s attention from writing every line to deciding what should be built and how to verify it. Your judgment still matters enormously; you just have another tool for turning that judgment into working software.

r001.rationale: The response says that engineers can ask for a small function or describe a larger goal, with the model’s role changing accordingly. It also says that clarity about the request matters.

r002.rationale: It varies the scope of the request by task, but does not state that the appropriate frequency of interaction depends on the task.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes clearly specifying constraints and success criteria, but does not say that doing so enables the model to execute the task independently.
